Vignette: Breathing Poison

Boon-Nam is a 52-year-old Thai-American man who has worked as an HVAC technician for nearly two decades. He is methodical by nature, the kind of man who reads every manual twice and keeps his tools arranged in a precise order in the back of his service van. His colleagues have always regarded him as unflappable - someone who could troubleshoot a failing industrial chiller in a sweltering basement without breaking a sweat. That reputation feels like it belongs to a different person now.

Three years ago, Boon-Nam was contracted to service a refrigeration system in a commercial food processing facility. What no one told him - what the facility's own maintenance logs had apparently failed to document - was that a slow ammonia leak had been accumulating in the mechanical room for weeks. He entered the space alone, carrying only a standard respirator rated for particulates, not for toxic gas. Within minutes, his eyes were burning. By the time he understood what was happening, he had already inhaled a significant concentration of anhydrous ammonia. He remembers the sensation of his throat closing, the way the air seemed to turn solid inside his chest. He remembers crawling toward the door and not being certain he was going to reach it. A coworker found him collapsed in the corridor and called emergency services. He spent four days in the ICU and several more weeks recovering from chemical burns to his airways.

His pulmonologist tells him his lung function has largely stabilized, though he still experiences intermittent bronchospasms. But the damage Boon-Nam is most aware of is not the kind that shows up on a spirometry test.

He cannot enter a confined space without his heart beginning to slam against his ribs. The smell of anything chemical - cleaning products, car exhaust, even his wife's hair spray - can send him lurching backward, heart racing, hands shaking, convinced on some animal level that the air is trying to kill him again. He knows, rationally, that he is standing in his own kitchen. He knows this. And yet his body does not believe him.

Sleep is where the worst of it lives. He wakes most nights between two and four in the morning, gasping, certain he is back on that concrete floor. His wife, Malee, reaches for him in the dark, and he flinches before he recognizes her touch. He hates himself for that flinch. He does not tell her this.

At work, he has quietly begun refusing jobs that involve enclosed mechanical rooms or any system that handles refrigerants or industrial gases. He routes those calls to younger technicians, inventing reasons - scheduling conflicts, equipment certifications. His supervisor has not yet pressed him, but Boon-Nam knows the pattern is becoming visible. He has built his livelihood on being willing to go where the work is, and now there are places he simply cannot make himself go.

He describes a persistent sense of being sealed off from his own life. He sits at dinner with Malee and their adult daughter and watches them laugh at something on television, and he feels as though he is observing them through glass. He used to coach youth soccer on weekends. He stopped going without fully deciding to stop. He tells himself he is tired, and this is partly true, but the fuller truth is that the field is next to a park maintenance facility, and sometimes the groundskeepers use fertilizers that carry a faint chemical smell on the wind, and he cannot trust himself not to embarrass his family by running.

He is a proud man who immigrated to this country in his twenties with little and built something steady and real. He does not easily ask for help. He came to therapy, he says quietly, because his daughter told him she missed him - not his body at the dinner table, but him, the version of her father who used to be present. He is not sure that man still exists, but he is here, which he offers as evidence that some part of him believes otherwise.
